title: How Artificial Intelligence Disrupts Engineering Progression
gist: Alasdair Allan argues at QCon London that AI simultaneously stunts junior skill formation, converts programming into supervision, and slows entry-level hiring — so firms adopting AI coding tools are degrading the very pipeline that produces the seniors capable of supervising those tools; he cites METR's RCT showing experienced developers 19% slower with AI while believing they were 20% faster, and zero of fifteen AI-generated PRs mergeable on real open-source projects.

insights.claim: AI disrupts career progression by eliminating the learning opportunities at each rung while simultaneously letting people perform above their experience level, so the apparent productivity gain masks a hollowing of the skill ladder.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Firms measuring only output will miss a multi-year capability liability building on their balance sheet of talent.

insights.claim: Organizations racing to adopt AI coding tools are simultaneously degrading the pipeline that produces people capable of supervising those tools, because the people who can build good context for AI are those who accumulated context through years of craft.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A self-undermining adoption loop: the scarcity of qualified AI supervisors is the bottleneck that will price senior engineering labour over the next decade.
insights.quote: Organizations racing to adopt AI coding tools are simultaneously degrading the pipeline that produces people capable of supervising those tools.
insights.locator: Organizations racing to adopt AI coding tools

insights.claim: Hiring of young workers has slowed in AI-exposed occupations with no corresponding decrease in work for workers over 25, meaning the labour market effect shows up as non-hiring rather than layoffs.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Employment headline numbers will understate AI displacement because it manifests as suppressed entry-level hiring, not visible job cuts.
insights.quote: People weren’t being sacked; they just weren’t being hired in the first place.
insights.locator: The hiring of young workers has slowed

insights.claim: Allan predicts companies that deliberately preserve inefficient apprenticeship work — like medical residencies where you do the scut work because it teaches you — will be the ones that still have senior developers in ten years.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Deliberate training inefficiency becomes a competitive moat; watch which employers fund it versus which optimise it away.
insights.quote: Like medical residencies, you do the scut work because it teaches you, not because it’s efficient

insights.claim: METR's randomised controlled trial found experienced developers were 19% slower when using AI while believing they were 20% faster — a roughly 39-point gap between perceived and actual productivity.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Self-reported AI productivity gains from engineering orgs are unreliable inputs; demand measured throughput before underwriting AI-driven headcount plans.
insights.quote: METR’s randomised controlled trial found experienced developers were 19% slower with AI, while believing they were 20% faster.
insights.locator: InfoQ: What are the conclusions from studies

insights.claim: Anthropic research found junior engineers using AI scored 17% lower on mastery without finishing any faster, meaning they traded learning for no measurable output gain.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The cost of AI assistance for juniors is negative on both axes in this study — a hard argument for differentiated tool policies by seniority.
insights.quote: Anthropic found junior engineers using AI scored 17% lower on mastery without finishing any faster. They traded learning for nothing.
insights.locator: InfoQ: What are the conclusions from studies

insights.claim: Zero out of fifteen AI-generated pull requests were mergeable on real open-source projects despite passing automated tests, indicating test-passing is a weak proxy for production readiness.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Automated test pass rates are being used as AI-quality evidence and are demonstrably insufficient — a due-diligence red flag on agentic coding vendor claims.
insights.quote: Zero out of fifteen AI-generated PRs were mergeable on real open-source projects, despite passing automated tests. AI implements functionality. It fails at craft.
insights.locator: AI is genuinely useful for short, well-defined tasks

insights.claim: AI gains collapse as task complexity increases and the bottleneck migrates upstream to code review, exactly where senior judgment lives.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: If review becomes the constraint, tooling investment should shift from generation to verification — the underserved half of the market.
insights.quote: the gains collapse as complexity increases and the bottleneck migrates upstream to code review, exactly where senior judgment lives
insights.locator: AI is genuinely useful for short, well-defined tasks

insights.claim: Anthropic's own engineers use Claude in 59% of their daily work but can only fully delegate around 20%, and Allan argues the future of engineering jobs lives in that gap between generation and judgment.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The 59%-vs-20% delegation gap is a usable ceiling estimate for near-term AI substitution of engineering labour.
insights.quote: Anthropic’s engineers use Claude in 59% of their daily work, but can only fully delegate around 20%. That gap is where the jobs will live in the future, between generation and judgment.
insights.locator: InfoQ: How does the work that computer programmers do change

insights.claim: Allan reports 80 to 90% of engineering questions now go to AI rather than colleagues, bypassing the incidental learning that came from struggling through a problem with a mentor.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Mentorship traffic collapsing is a leading indicator of the skills gap that shows up in hiring markets three to five years later.
insights.quote: What concerns me is that 80 to 90% of engineering questions now go to AI rather than colleagues.
insights.locator: InfoQ: How does the work that computer programmers do change

insights.claim: Using AI requires supervision and supervision requires coding skills, so AI productivity benefits may come at the cost of the very skills needed to validate AI-written code.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Validation capacity, not generation capacity, is the constraint that determines how far AI coding can safely scale in an org.

insights.claim: The career pipeline was built for people who write code and has not been rebuilt for people who supervise systems.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A structural gap that creates demand for new training products, certifications and career frameworks aimed at supervision skills.
insights.quote: The career pipeline was built for people who write code. We haven’t rebuilt it for people who supervise systems.
insights.locator: InfoQ: How does the work that computer programmers do change

themes.theme: Blackfield systems and what AI cannot read

insights.claim: Allan frames most engineering as 'blackfield' — legacy systems under high load on an agreed deprecation path nobody has time to execute, where the spec was never written or was invalidated by decades of undocumented decisions and business rules encoded in conditions that outlived everyone who understood them.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for judging where AI coding tools will and won't deliver: greenfield demos do not map to the blackfield majority of real work.
insights.quote: Most engineering is what people call blackfield: legacy systems under high load, on a deprecation path everyone agrees on, but no one has time to execute
insights.locator: Most engineering is what people call blackfield

insights.claim: AI agents can read code and test documentation but cannot read production — they cannot look at years of request patterns to understand which code paths are load-bearing in ways the code itself does not reveal.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Identifies the durable human moat and, inversely, the product gap: tooling that feeds production telemetry into agent context.
insights.quote: AI agents can read the code, test the documentation, but what they can’t do is read production
insights.locator: AI agents can read the code

insights.claim: Junior engineers are not building intuition for what is right about code because they will not spend years reading legacy codebases or debugging 3 a.m. production incidents — they will point an AI agent at it and ask for a summary.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Pattern recognition that used to accrue automatically now needs deliberate manufacture, which costs money nobody has budgeted.
insights.quote: Junior engineers won’t spend years reading legacy codebases or debugging production incidents at 3 a.m. They’ll just point the AI agent at it and ask it to summarize.
insights.locator: The pattern recognition veteran coders carry

insights.claim: Allan explicitly says the field is at the diagnosis stage rather than the solution stage and he does not have the full answer for building engineers in the AI era.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: No settled playbook exists yet — an open market for whoever operationalises a credible answer to AI-era engineering development.
insights.quote: I don’t have the full answer. We’re at the diagnosis stage, not the solution stage.
insights.locator: InfoQ: What are your suggestions for building engineers

insights.claim: Allan's concrete prescriptions are structured learning paths with deliberate rotation through fundamentals, measuring understanding rather than velocity by watching how people think rather than what they produce, and treating context as infrastructure by writing documentation that reads like onboarding for a senior engineer new to the codebase.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Shifts engineering metrics away from velocity dashboards — a change in what management tooling needs to measure.
insights.quote: We need to measure understanding, not velocity. Watch how people think, not what they produce.
insights.locator: InfoQ: What are your suggestions for building engineers

insights.claim: Allan frames AI as a tool and not a teacher, and using it to skip understanding as borrowing against your future.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A framing to apply when evaluating AI-native training claims from edtech and developer-tool vendors.
insights.quote: AI is a tool, not a teacher. Using it to skip understanding is borrowing against your future.
insights.locator: We need to set honest expectations
